en: It is stated "out of conceit" (*abhimānāt*) to indicate that it is more appropriate to postulate other [distinct] causalities,
since there is parsimony (*lāghava*) in postulating a single one.

If [the probandum] is not included among the established categories of entities (*padārtha*), then the "not being included among the six categories of existence" mentioned as the root [reason] cannot function as a valid reason, because it would be inconclusive (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to non-existence (*abhāva*). Nor can the "not being included among non-existences" mentioned by the phrase "nor non-existence" serve as a reason, because it would be inconclusive with respect to the category of existence (*bhāva*). Therefore, another reason must be stated.

He completes [the sentence] with "ṣaḍbhāvān" (the six states). Regarding the word "tatra" (therein): the meaning is "in the reason already stated. The sense of the locative case is that of being a constituent part (*ghaṭakatvam*). And its connection is with the end of the word "satya" (truth). As for the phrase "hi hetau": the meaning is that the word *hi* expresses a reason.
This is because the locative case here has the sense of "denoting" (*vācakatva*). Thus, it is as follows:
The intended meaning is that, because there is no distinction from the reason (*hetu*), it does not possess the specific quality of being included within the six categories (*ṣaḍbhāvapadārtha*).
Nor, when "reason" is stated in this way,

is there a deficiency due to the failure to state the correlate (*anvayin*) that defines the nature of the reason, since the expectation arises as to "where [is it]?"— that is, what is the locus of the reason.

It should be stated [as follows]: by supplying the phrase "in the case of that which possesses the reason" (*uktahetau*) from the preceding context, the intended meaning is the cognition that similarity is the locus of the absence of being included within the six categories—which is qualified by the absence of being included within the categories other than the stated reason and its non-differentiated [counter-positive]. And here, it is only the two absences—namely, the absence of being included within the category of existence (*bhāva*) and the absence of being included within the category of non-existence (*abhāva*)—taken together [that constitute the definition].

It should be understood that the status of being a cause belongs to each of the two— existence and non-existence— individually, because [the alternative] would involve a logical deviation (*vyabhicāra*).

And this, by implication, serves as a further reason for establishing the status of the two combined absences mentioned in the root text as a distinct category (*atirikta-padārtha*), since the possibility of their being a cause is only established when supplemented by this additional reason.
It should be noted that it is inappropriate to explain the passage beginning with "taddhi" as being intended merely to refute the non-establishment of the qualifier-qualified relationship;
for [the phrase] "provided that it resides in something other than a universal" includes "even in a universal," by which the term "other than a universal" is also [implied].

The intention is that this meaning is obtained because [the definition] has been compiled [from various sources]. "By that" means by the inclusion of the property of subsisting in both the universal and its opposite.

Now, universality (sāmānyatva) consists in being eternal while being inherent in many; and since that [eternality] takes the form of not being the counter-positive of either destruction or prior non-existence, it is indeed of the nature of an absence (abhāva).
How is there deviation? And it is not the case that, due to a lack of a deciding factor (*vinigamanā-viraheṇa*), [the definition] fails;

for even "inherence in multiple things" (*aneka-samavetatva*) can constitute the nature of being a universal (*sāmānyatva*), and this consists in being the counter-correlate (*pratiyogitva*) of an inherence relation whose relata (*anuyogika*) are multiple.

It should not be argued that there is a deviation (vyabhicāra) because the nature of a universal consists in its being a specific relation of identity with its own form; for even so, since the relation of locus and located (ādhārādheyabhāva) is not admitted in the case of non-difference, and thus the existence of subsistence in it is absent from the universal, no deviation can possibly arise. Nor is it [the case that] universality...
It must be stated that what is intended is precisely a cognition whose mode (*prakāra*) is the state of being a universal (*sāmānyatva*). If that were the case,

then because a cognition having a universal as its object is related to the universal by way of being its object (*viṣayatā*), and because it also subsists in something other than the universal (namely, the self), the inclusion of the "satyanta" (the truth-condition) would still be necessary.

Because the state of deviation remains as it was; because, due to the absence of a purpose such as the exclusion of deviation, it is inappropriate to intend "relatedness" (*saṃbandhitva*) in place of "subsistence" (*vṛttitva*) merely for the sake of making the term "real" (*sat*) meaningful; therefore, [this refers] to that which is defined by generality (*sāmānya*).
Since a subsistence delimited by any other relation is unestablished,
the reason must be stated as "subsistence in general, delimited by the relation of identity (*svarūpasaṃbandha*).
And since such subsistence in general does not exist in the case of "generality-ness" (*sāmānyatva*), the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is impossible.

This is indeed correct; for even by one who does not assert that similarity (*sādṛśya*) is an additional entity, it must be admitted that it functions as a qualifier (*prakāra*) through the relation of identity (*svarūpa-sambandha*), and even by one who asserts that it consists in the possession of many common properties, it [functions] through its very nature (*svarūpeṇa*).

The mode-of-being (*prakāratā*) must be accepted, because there can be no dispute regarding experience, and because it is inappropriate for a single-form cognition to possess that mode-of-being through multiple relations. For this very reason, the author of the treatise also did not state [the definition] as "that which possesses many properties residing in that [object], while being different from it."
If it is argued that [the definition] has been followed up to the limit of "possessing many properties residing in that [subject]," and thus,

in order to avoid the fallacy of *svarūpāsiddhi* (unestablished nature) regarding similarity (*sādṛśya*), one must necessarily accept that the probans (*hetu*) is simply "residingness" (*vṛttitva*) as delimited by a relation defined by a universal (*sāmānya*) established in both systems, and therefore there is no *vyabhicāra* (inconstancy)— we say: no.

Since the cognition "the universal possesses universality" involves the apprehension of the universal as the locus of universality, and since it is difficult to define universality as something distinct from the universal itself, [universality] is related to itself by way of identity (svarūpa-sambandha).

The property of residing in itself (*svavṛttitva*) must necessarily be admitted, because everyone accepts it as such in cases involving the absence of an absence that serves as its own locus. By this very method, the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) to be mentioned later regarding [the property] "knowability" (*prameyatva*) and so forth should also be understood, based on the cognition: "Everything possesses knowability."

Because it is necessary that knowability (*prameyatva*), which is the very nature of valid cognition (*pramā*), exists through the relation of identity (*svarūpa-sambandha*); and because if objectivity (*viṣayatā*) were identical with the object itself, it would contradict the experience that "knowability is one and the same everywhere. Furthermore, if knowability were the nature of cognition, [it would exist] through the relation of identity.
The sense is that because [the property] exists in both the general and its other, deviation is necessary.

One might raise the objection: "But since the nature of being an entity (bhāvatva) consists in existing by way of either one of the two relations, the reason is present there, and thus there is deviation. He dispels this doubt with the words: "And as for being an entity... (bhāvatve ca).

Nor should it be argued that even so, the deviation (vyabhicāra) regarding the duality residing in the pot and the pot-ness remains unavoidable— since, even if its status as a number is impossible, an *apekṣābuddhi* must necessarily exist in the form of an essential relation (*svarūpasambandha*) with respect to that which possesses duality, in order to account for the cognition of duality. This is because [the opponent’s position] is untenable.
This is because it is accepted that even "being other than that which subsists distributively" (vyāsajyavṛttyanyatva) serves as a qualification of the reason (*hetu*).

Furthermore, "subsisting distributively" (*vyāsajyavṛttitva*) is defined as the state of possessing non-pervasion (*aparyāpti*) delimited by a property that subsists in only one [of two or more]; thus, there is nothing at all that is untenable. In reality, however...

The intention of the author of the root-text (*mūlakṛt*) is that the reason (*hetu*) is precisely "residing in a universal as delimited by the relation of identity" (*svarūpasaṃbandhāvaccchinnasāmānyavṛttitvam*). However, the mention of "subsisting by its own nature" (*svarūpasataḥ*) is for the purpose of dispelling the objection that if similarity resided only in the universal, there would be no cognition of similarity to the moon in the face and so forth.

Because it exists in both the general and its opposite, this [definition] is merely a restatement (anuvādaka) and not intended by the author of the root text (*mūlakṛt*) as the delimiting condition of the probans (*hetutāvacchedakatva*). Nor should it be argued that there is thus a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to "generality-ness" (*sāmānyatva*), which is the very nature of generality;
for [the definition applies] to the state of inhering in many, in accordance with the cognition of the relation between locus and located (*ādhārādheyabhāva*).

For it must be admitted that existence (*sattā*) is the universal precisely because its nature is eternality. Likewise, "knowability" (*prameyatva*) is not cognition itself—since that would contradict the meaning of the suffixes and other elements [in the word *prameya*] which signify an object—but rather the state of being an object of cognition (*pramāviṣayatva*). And thus, knowability, being of the nature of objecthood (*viṣayatā*), [is distinct] with respect to each particular object.

Since it is impossible for [the property] to reside in both the universal and its other at any given objecthood (*viṣayatā*) by virtue of being distinct, there is no possibility of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) even with respect to knowability (*prameyatva*); thus, the qualification "negative" (*vyatirekitva*) in the reason (*hetu*) is indeed purposeless. However, as for that which consists of the nature of the object...

Since objecthood (*viṣayatā*) exists as a general property (*sāmānyavṛtti*) by virtue of its relation of identity (*svarūpasaṃbandha*), the qualification "not delimited by the nature of objecthood (*viṣayatātva*)" and so forth must be added to the definition of being a general property in order to exclude deviation (*vyabhicāra*). Furthermore, in this way, even duality (*dvitva*) and the like are nothing other than the objecthood of a comparative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*).

Nor is there any deviation [in the reason] even in the case of relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*), because the subsistence of [the property of being] a subject (*viṣayavṛttitva*) in a cognition has never been established anywhere; therefore, one may also qualify the reason by the phrase "being distinct from a universal" (*sāmānyabhinnatva*),
since the probans is possible in the case of similarity (*sādṛśya*), as it does not exist in a universal.
We consider it logical that even the word "api" (also/even) is meaningful for the sake of obtaining this [result].

Regarding the phrase "as a positive entity" (*bhāvatvena*): one might object that being perceived as a positive entity remains intact even in the case of a non-entity (*abhāva*) for a person under delusion; however, since [the latter] is not included within non-entities, this [objection does not apply].

In order to dispel the suspicion that the reason (*hetu*) is inconclusive (*vyabhicārī*), he states its meaning as "because it is being cognized" (*pramīyamāṇatvāt*). [The phrase] "at some time or other" (*yadākadācit*) refers to even during the state when the jewel (*maṇi*) is present, by way of delimitation to a previous time.

The point is that there would be the undesirable consequence of burning from fire characterized by the property of being co-located with the absence of a jewel (*maṇyabhāva*). [Objection: But surely, it is precisely the presence of the cause as qualified by the delimiting factor of its causal capacity (*kāraṇatāvacchedaka*) that is the determinant of the production of the effect.

In that locus, during the state when the absence of the jewel is present, there is no occurrence of burning because of the absence of the substratumhood qualified by the absence of the jewel through the relation of co-location (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*); therefore, he says: "qualified by the delimitors of causality" (*kāraṇatāvacchedakāvalīḍhe*). This means "characterized by the delimiters of causality" (*kāraṇatāvacchedakopalakṣita*).
Otherwise, if the cognition of the qualifier— being of the nature of a qualified cognition— were the cause of the qualified cognition by way of the relation of objectivity (*viṣayitā*),
there would result the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of a qualified cognition produced by a cognition of a qualifier that is past or future.

[The opponent says: "But surely, it is not the qualifier itself that is the delimiting condition (*kāraṇatāvacchedaka*) of causality by way of the relation of being the object (*viṣayitā-sambandha*), but rather the objectivity (*viṣayitā*) as determined by the qualifier; and since this objectivity exists only at the same time as the cognition, [the cause] qualified by the delimiting condition of causality..."
Since there is no deficiency even if [the absence of the jewel] is the cause of the production of the effect, he says "in the absence of the jewel" out of a sense of unease.

Regarding the phrase "being cumbersome": even if one accepts that both the state of being fire (*vahni*) and the state of being the absence of the jewel (*maṇyabhāva*) are causes, there are still only two causalities, though they are delimited by lighter properties.

The point is that if [fire] were a cause by way of being qualified by the absence of a jewel (*maṇyabhāva*) and so forth, there would result two causal powers delimited by heavy (complex) properties. Now, one might object: "In this case, the status of the jewel as an obstructor (*pratibandhaka*) would be untenable, for it is only that which disrupts the causes [of an effect] that is considered an obstructor."
Because the jewel acts as an obstacle and because the absence of the jewel has not perished, he says: "And thus...

[referring to] "of the sublating cognition" (*bādhajñānasya*). In a case where, immediately after the inferential consideration (*parāmarśa*), there is a sublating certainty in the form of ordinary perception (*laukikapratyakṣa*), at the second moment following the arising of that sublating certainty...

The destruction of the power residing in the *parāmarśa* (the subsumptive reflection) must be stated. And thus, it would have to be said that at the third moment following the arising of the sublation (*bādha*), there is an obstruction to the inferential cognition (*anumiti*) by that [sublation]. But that is not possible, because the non-arising of the inference prior to that [third moment] is already possible due to the absence of the *parāmarśa* itself.

The point is that [if one were to accept such a power], an inference would result even in the second moment of the sublation, because the reflective awareness (parāmarśa) qualified by that power exists prior to it. As for the phrase "but not something additional":
this is because there is no logical justification for accepting an additional power when the absence of the gem (maṇyabhāva) itself serves as the cause.

The sense is that the nature of being an obstructor (pratibandhakatva), defined as the state of being the counter-positive of an absence that has become a cause, is impossible in the case of a [fire-]jewel (maṇi). Regarding the phrase "absence of the cause":
since there is no conventional usage of the term "obstructor" with respect to the absence of a cause, [the obstructor must exist] while the cause is present. (Rāmarudrī)

The point is that since only that which causes the non-arising of an effect is designated as an "obstructer" (pratibandhaka), there is no possibility of the undesired consequence [of over-extension]. As for the phrase "and in the case of a jar, etc.":
the point is that it would follow that a thing itself would be an obstructer to its own production.

Since the absence of an obstructer (*pratibandhakābhāva*) is a cause by virtue of its existence at the time of the effect (*kāryakālavṛttitva*), there is no undesirable consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*) here either. [The opponent says: "An absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) is that which is distinct from a positive entity (*bhāva*). [The author replies: By taking the nature of fire itself as the absence of the absence of fire, [the definition applies] to fire.

The term "distinct from a positive entity" (bhāvabhinnah) is used to prevent the contingency of [a thing] being an obstacle to itself; the term "absolute absence" (atyantābhāvaḥ) is used to prevent the contingency of prior absence (prāgabhāvaḥ) being an obstacle to itself.
Although absolute absence is defined as being a relational absence (saṃsargābhāvaḥ) that is eternal (nitya), this [definition] does not [apply here].

In the *Bhāṣāpariccheda* and other such works, the nature of non-existence (*abhāvatva*) is defined as being distinct from existence (*bhāva*); however, in the present context, absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāvatva*) does not consist of that [definition] involving the exclusion of existence. Rather, it is the state of having a counter-correlate (*sapratiyogikatva*), provided that it is distinct from mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) and distinct from destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) and prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*). Therefore, it is not distinct from existence.

Thus, [the rule] would be redundant; for this very reason, the restriction that "where the locative case follows the word denoting the counter-correlative (anuyogin), absolute non-existence (atyantābhāva) is conveyed by the negative particle (nañ)" is also justified. Otherwise, in cases such as "there is no absence of a jar on the ground" (*bhūtale ghaṭābhāvo nāsti*), the negative particle could not convey absolute non-existence at all.
It should be understood that this refers to the state of being an object of cognition (*bodhyatva*). Regarding the phrase "is refuted" (*parāsta*):

one might argue that, in order to avoid the aforementioned undesirable consequence (*āpatti*), the qualification of the causal capacity (*kāraṇatā*) should simply be "being delimited by the relation of spatial qualification" (*daiśika-viśeṣaṇatā-sambandha-avacchinnatva*).

In that case, since positive entities (*bhāva*) are not causes by way of the relation of spatial qualification, [the definition] would apply to things other than positive entities (*bhāvabhinnatva*). Even so—[this is the objection]. *Rāmarudrī*: [This is the end of the objection. Final Answer: The final answer is the translation provided above. I hope it is correct.

It should not be said that [this relation] is not to be accepted as a cause; for since positive entities (bhāvas) also possess spatial qualification (*daiśika-viśeṣaṇatā*) by virtue of being qualified by conjunction with the eye (*cakṣuḥ-saṃyukta-viśeṣaṇatā*) and so forth, it is necessary.
Furthermore, this [relation]—in the form of a qualification that determines the cognition "this is here"—is not cumbersome.

The object of meditation [is this]: because it is not included [within any other category]. The sense is that since it is difficult to state a single "stimulating" nature (*utejakatva*) in the case of gems, mantras, great medicinal herbs, and so forth, and because it is impossible for it to be a universal (*jāti*) due to its overlapping with earthness (*pṛthivītva*) and other such properties.
[Objection: "But in this way, it is impossible for the absence of the jewel qualified by the absence of the stimulator to be the cause, because there is no single, uniform stimulator.
To this, he says: "of the absence of the jewel qualified by the aggregate (kūṭa) of its absences."
If the absence of the jewel qualified by the absence of the stimulator were the cause,

then even during the state of the stimulator in the form of a mantra, since the mantra resides in space, its absence would exist in that same location where the fire is present; thus, [the required condition] would hold through the relation of co-location (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).

There would be the undesirable consequence that burning does not occur because of the existence of the jewel qualified by the absence of its stimulator. Furthermore, under the view that a substance exists non-pervasively (avyāpyavṛtti) through conjunction, there would be the contingency of burning even while the jewel is present, since the absence of the jewel exists through conjunction at some particular locus; such is the doubt.
He refutes [the objection] by stating: "In this regard, it should be understood as follows. Regarding the phrase "being a qualifier of an absence":

the sense is that since burning consists of the nature of destruction (dhvaṃsa), its production occurs precisely as a qualifier. Regarding the phrase "either being the object of reference (uddeśyatā) or spatial qualification (daiśika-viśeṣaṇatā)": [it means] that the mantra [exerts its influence] solely through the relation of being the object of reference.
Because [the absence of the obstructer] exists in a location other than the locus of the action, the property of being the "intended object" (uddeśyatā) is introduced.

Since there is no burning even when an intensifier such as a gem is present—because that absence [of the obstructer] exists through a certain type of conjunction—the property of "spatial qualification" (daiśika-viśeṣaṇatā) is introduced. (Rāmarudrī, p. 3).

The point is that, because [the absence] is a delimiting attribute (*vaiśeṣaṇatā*) of the burner, the substance does not have a non-pervasive occurrence; thus, there is no impossibility of burning. And this was stated while accepting a delimiting attribute common to both presence and absence.
"Of the jewel, etc."—by "etc.," the inclusion of mantras and so forth is intended. For this very reason...
The objectivehood (uddeśyatā) enters into the relation-limit. However, when spatial qualification (daiśika-viśeṣaṇatā) is introduced in place of conjunction, the reasoning is exactly as stated.
"The state of being a triad-dyad" means an individual dimension residing in a triad-dyad.
Therefore, there is no flaw even though the state of being a "long dyad" exists in various dyads.

Now, one might object that since the subject (*pakṣa*) is specifically the long [substance] qualified by largeness (*mahattva*), there is no fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*); to this, he says: "of the frying-pan lid," and so forth.

Even if one takes the conjunction with the fuel of a large fire-atom (tryaṇuka) as the subject, there is no "proving what is already established" (siddhasādhana) regarding a large fire; therefore, it is specified as "conjunction with a self possessing unseen merit" (adṛṣṭavat).
Since unseen merit is a cause for every effect through its relation as a conjunction with its own substratum, [it is mentioned] by way of that relation.

The sense is that conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is also a cause. Although the example of the self (*ātman*) here is inappropriate—since there is no evidence for its being a producer of burning—nevertheless, this was stated with the intention of asserting that in every effect, the agent alone is the cause. Or else...

In this context, "the capacity to produce burning" does not mean being the cause of burning (dāhakāraṇatva), but rather being the determinant of burning (dāhaprayojakatva). Furthermore, this [determinative capacity] is common to both direct causes and their causes; it consists in a relation of essential identity (svarūpasaṃbandha) and thus remains intact even in the case of the efficient cause (kṛtikāraṇa) which is the cause of all effects. This should be kept in mind. As for the phrase "because it is logical": this is merely prima facie. Regarding power (śakti):...

It should be understood that because [the effect] possesses production and destruction by virtue of being destroyed by an obstacle and being produced by the removal of that [obstacle], there would result the fallacy of an excessive complexity (gaurava) due to the necessity of postulating infinite powers. Regarding the phrase "by a specific defect," the meaning is "in the form of unseen merit/demerit (adṛṣṭa)" and so forth; otherwise...
The sense is that, even in your view, there would be the undesirable consequence (āpatti) of the perception of a capacity residing in the fire-wood (indhana).
[Objection: "Because that is not a fault.

[Response: Because [the definition of pervasion] involves both relations: the relation of co-location with itself (svasāmānādhikaraṇya) and the relation of co-location with its own absence (svābhāvasāmānādhikaraṇya).

The sense is that there is no evidence for the property of being a "jāti qualified by a jāti" (jātiviśiṣṭajātitva) being pervaded by the absence of being the counter-positive of an absolute non-existence that is co-locus with itself; therefore, there is no evidence that *sāṃkarya* (overlapping) is a subverter of *jātitva*. [Regarding the phrase] "due to the impossibility of being a delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) by its own nature" (*svarūpataḥ*): [this refers to] that which is other than a *jāti* being [a delimiting factor] by its own nature.

Because manifestation is not admitted [as a separate entity]. The sense is that there is a rule that whatever manifests by its own nature (*svarūpataḥ*) is precisely what constitutes the delimiting condition (*avacchedakatva*) by its own nature.

Regarding the phrase "of that which consists in a relation of identity" (*svarūpa-sambandha-rūpāyāḥ*): the sense is that it is impossible for there to be a difference [in causal power] based on a difference in the delimiters of causality (*kāraṇatāvacchedaka*), because [causal power] takes the form of the specific individuality of each respective cause (*tat-tat-kāraṇa-vyakti*). [This applies to] a [causal power] that is distinct [from the cause itself].

Thus [it means]: "of that which is distinct from the seven categories. Because such a causality would differ due to the difference in its delimiting factors (*avacchedakatā*), there would result the cumbersome assumption of multiple individual instances of form; therefore, it is more appropriate to postulate a single causality as determined by multiple delimiting factors.

The state [of being] is as follows: it should be noted that the nature of causality, which consists in pervasiveness, is distinct according to its various limiting factors (avacchedakatva) and so forth, because it is constituted by a property that does not serve as the delimitor for the complete distribution (paryāpti) of the counter-correlativity (pratiyogitā). This is also an elliptical indication (upalakṣaṇa) regarding the difference [of things] in terms of their specific individuality (tadvyaktitva).

The state [of being]. Because it would result in the fallacy of impossibility if one were to take a specific individual jar as the subject. Even though, since inherence lacks any other member of its own class when considered under the form of a property that differentiates categories,

it cannot be the primary qualificand in the inference of a difference from its own class— and thus there is no over-extension of the definition of *viśeṣa* (ultimate particularity) to inherence— nevertheless...
