Nevertheless, it should be noted that there is no over-extension (ativyāpti), because the qualifying portion (viśeṣyadala) of the definition— consisting of being different from that [object], while possessing the property of being distinct from itself yet belonging to the same class as itself, or else the property of inherence (samavetatva), or else the property of being distinct from inherence— is introduced as the object of such an inference. This applies to the case of inference.

The qualification "not preceded by a desire to prove" (*siṣādhayiṣānutaratva*) must also be included; otherwise, once the difference between particulars (*viśeṣa*) has been established by [the reason] "being inherent in this particular atom" (*etat-paramāṇu-samavetatva*),
even if one were to infer the difference of one particular from another particular by means of that mark through a desire to prove it— [the definition would still fail].

It is not impossible. [Objection: But surely, by the verse stating that "the ultimate resides in eternal substances," the definition of a *viśeṣa* (ultimate particularity) has been stated as being "that which, while being ultimate, resides in eternal substances. In that context, "ultimacy" (*antyatva*) is simply the state of being differentiated per se; it is called "ultimate" (*antya*) because it exists at the end (*ante*), that is, at the conclusion (*avasāne*) of differentiators.
Thus, since the analysis of the term [tattva] yields the meaning that "reality" (tattva) is simply the state of being excluded from others (vyāvṛttatva),

and since it is possible for this very state of being excluded by itself (svato vyāvṛttatva) to serve as the definition, the qualification "subsisting in eternal substances" (nityadravyavṛttitva) is redundant;
for even inherence (samavāya) subsists in eternal substances.
Furthermore, it is impossible for [the definition] to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to *samavāya*, because even the property of being a substratum (*vṛttitva*) is unestablished there.

Nor should it be argued that "being a substratum" is intended here as nothing other than "being inherent" (*samavetatva*), and thus that very term serves to exclude over-extension to *samavāya*; for even so, [the problem remains].

With the intention that, since it would be possible to avoid over-extension (*ativyāpti*) there by the mere fact of being inherent (*samavetatva*), the inclusion of "eternal substances" (*nityadravya*) would be unavoidable as redundant, he says:
"The statement of the locus of the particulars. [He adds] "of a property that is not excluded," because it is intended to be the means of establishing difference (*bheda*).
The meaning is: "of a property unknown as residing in that [atom]," because it is impossible for it to be a differentiator;

that is to say, because it lacks the capacity to establish its difference from others. In this context, regarding "this atom-ness" (*etat-paramāṇutva*) and so forth, there would be a requirement for another differentiator; that is, regarding this atom-ness, there would be a requirement for another probans to establish its non-residence in other atoms.

"Because of non-termination" means because of the consequence of infinite regress (*anavasthā-prasaṅga*). "This consequence" means a consequence consisting of the consequence of infinite regress. "Of that particularity" [means]:
by the very means of knowledge that apprehends the subject (*dharmin*), the distinction of the atom must be made known by some inferential mark (*liṅga*).

Because it possesses the nature of being a division—just as the division of a jar is known through the division of its shards—by means of this inference which establishes a specific distinction. "By way of being established" means by way of being established as having the form of being covered by another atom, precisely as a differentiation that is intrinsic and independent of any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). This is the meaning of the term "inference" (*anumiti*).

If the particular (*viśeṣa*) were to reside in another atom, it would be impossible for it to establish the distinction from that other atom; thus, because it would fail to function as a differentiator, the very existence of the particular could not be established.
This realization of the logical inconsistency, acting as an auxiliary to the inferential cognition (*parāmarśa*), [leads to the conclusion] that [the particular] does not reside in any other atom.
The meaning is that this is because the particular (*viśeṣa*) has been established. He concludes with "And thus" (*evaṃ ca*).
"In the form of the substratum" means in the form of the atoms that serve as the substrata for color and so forth. "By the particular" means by that which differentiates. Now, [an objection]:...

He dispels the doubt as to how that which is itself non-exclusive can be an exclusive differentiator by stating "of the substratum. "Not there" means not in the case of God (Īśvara) and space (ākāśa).
"The distinction" is [established] by the very terms "eternal knowledge" and "sound."
The meaning is that there is no purpose for a *viśeṣa* (ultimate particularity) in those two [space and time], since their mutual distinction from other eternal substances is already established.

The section ending with "Īśvara... and beginning with "āhuḥ" represents the view of the *ekadeśins* (partial adherents), and therein, the mutual distinction between space, time, ether, and so forth, is established.
Since it is not established that the eternally existent knowledge and sound are excluded from time and so forth,

it is impossible to prove the distinction of time and so forth by means of them; however, since the particularity [of the self] is established by the very means of cognition that apprehends the subject (dharmin),
it is possible to prove that distinction by means of that particularity itself— it is for the purpose of indicating this underlying unease [with the former position] that [the author] states this.
It has been stated [by others]:

"Since the difference from a specific water-atom existing in a specific earth-atom can be inferred by virtue of its inherence in earth, there is no lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) in that case for the property of being 'excluded by itself' (*svato-vyāvṛttatva*); therefore, [the definition] must be 'the inference of a difference from what is of its own kind' (*svasajātīya-bheda-anumiti*)."

He says that the meaning should be described as "the inference of the difference of all things other than itself and of its own genus"; however, that is weak, because the difference between an earth atom and a water atom cannot be established without a *viśeṣa* (ultimate particularity). For even if there were no difference between an earth atom and a water atom, [the properties of] water-ness and earth-ness [would remain distinct].
Although it can be said that the distinction between those two is indeed established because of the resulting confusion [of definitions],
nevertheless, in order to exclude the impossibility [of the definition applying to inference],
the qualification "not following from a desire to prove" (*siṣādhayiṣā-anuttaratva*) is necessary for inference.
It should be understood that, without a distinction between the specific qualities of an earth-atom and a water-atom,
the exclusion of the earth-atom's specific quality from the water-atom cannot be established; since the inference of a distinction between specific qualities— which depends upon that establishment—
must be accepted precisely because of the desire to prove it (siṣādhayiṣā), there is no possibility of the definition being too narrow (avyāpti).
He presents the view of the moderns with the words "the moderns, however. The phrase "they say" indicates the manifestation of a lack of satisfaction [with that view];
the seed of that [dissatisfaction] is the inference: "The part of a triad (tryaṇuka) possesses parts, because it is the originator of something large," as stated in the Rāmarudrī.

It should be understood that since the establishment of even a non-distinct atom is possible, the distinctness of eternal substances is precisely unestablished by the means of knowledge that apprehends the subject (*dharmigrāhakapramāṇa*). In this regard, it must be noted that, according to the reasoning stated previously, when inferring difference, it is necessary to include the condition of "not being preceded by a desire to prove" (*siṣādhayiṣānutaratva*).
The inclusion of the condition "having a probans distinct from itself" is fruitless;
for it is impossible to have a desire to prove (*siṣādhayiṣā*) one's own difference from others when that [difference] is already established by itself.

This is because it is impossible to prove the difference of one particular (*viśeṣa*) from another particular by means of that very particular which is non-different from the other particulars, and thus the establishment [of the probandum] is necessarily required whenever there is proof (*siddhi*).

Because inference is possible through the very desire to establish [the object]. Furthermore, the description of the author's intention—that the postulation of *viśeṣa* (particularity) is solely for the sake of establishing the mutual difference between atoms—is also inconsistent; for the difference between atoms must be made known by some inferential mark (*liṅga*).

Since the particularity (*viśeṣa*) must be established by the aforementioned inference, the distinction between two atoms can only be proven once that particularity is established; for only when the distinction between two atoms is established can one take them as the subject (*pakṣa*) and infer their particularity. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the subject being unestablished, which leads to the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*).
Furthermore, the statement by the author of the *Mūla*— beginning with "of jars and so forth, down to dyads"—
that the mutual difference between jars and other such objects is to be inferred from the difference in their shards (*kapāla*), is also inconsistent,
because the mutual difference between jars and so forth is established through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). In reality, however:

In passages such as "of jars and so forth, down to dyads," regarding the phrase "due to the difference among their respective parts" (*tattadavayavabhedāt*), the meaning of the ablative case is precisely "being the cause" (*prayuktatvam*), and not "being the indicator" (*jñāpyatvam*). This state of being the cause consists in an essential relation (*svarūpasambandha*);
that "the difference in the whole follows from the difference in the parts" is attested by common experience. And thus:

When the existence of two atoms is established through the impossibility of otherwise accounting for the production of a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*), their distinction is proven by means of an inference such as: "The distinction between those two [atoms] must be caused by something [else], because it is a distinction, like the distinction of a jar caused by the distinction of its potsherds. Through the force of the sublation of contrary positions (*itarabādha*) in such an inference, the distinction consisting of a specific quality (*viśeṣa*) residing in the atoms is established.

The fundamental purport [of the text] is that "the particular (viśeṣa) is established. Now, one might raise the objection: "Even if there is a distinction among particulars, since another inferential cause could be postulated for that, an infinite regress would result. In response to this doubt, it is stated:
"But that [particular] is excluded by itself. For a particular possesses a distinction that is produced by nothing other than itself.
The meaning is that it does not possess a difference induced by a further internal distinction residing therein. Thus,
self-exclusion (*svato-vyāvṛttatvam*) is precisely the state of being a differentiator of its own substratum— which is established by itself and is the cause of the cognition of its own class-mates.
"Lighter than the former as well"—thus everything is consistent. Regarding the phrase "the word 'jar' and the word 'potsherd,' etc.":

the meaning is "the words 'jar' and so forth, and the words 'potsherd' and so forth. One might raise the objection that there is a deficiency in the root text because the nature of *samavāya* (inherence) has not been stated regarding the relation between eternal substances and their specific qualities.

He refutes [the objection] with the words "and because of [the nature of] the universal" (jāteśca). Now, one might raise the following doubt: if the definition of a permanent relation (*nityasaṃbandha*) is characterized by coexistence (*samakālatva*), then there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to relations such as the essential identity (*svarūpasaṃbandha*) that a universal possesses with its own self, since such relations lack the property of being a substance (*dravyatva*). To address this suspicion:

He refutes [the objection] with the words "and the relation... [stating]: "[The relation] is distinct from its relata. Thus, the definition of inherence (*samavāya*) is: being a relation while being distinct from the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) and the substratum (*anuyogin*), and being eternal. Therefore, [this definition does not apply] to the relation of essential identity (*svarūpa-sambandha*), which consists of the counter-correlate and the substratum themselves.

There is no over-extension [of the definition]. Furthermore, in this context, due to parsimony (*lāghava*), there is only one single relation for the absence of substanceness (*dravyatva*) and so forth—namely, the absence of substanceness itself—and for jars and the like, there is only one single temporal relation with the Great Time (*mahākāla*), because the Great Time is one; thus, it is a relation of essential nature (*svarūpa-sambandha*).

It should be understood that there is a distinction: in some cases it has the nature of a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), and in others the nature of a sub-correlate (*anuyogin*). Furthermore, the property of being a relation (*saṃbandhatva*) consists simply in possessing a relational objective content (*sāṃsargika-viṣayatā*).
Regarding the phrase "only between two substances," this refers to conjunction (*saṃyoga*) in general as belonging to substance.

The sense is that [it is] because of being an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*). Now, an objection: according to the view of the moderns who maintain the plurality of inherence (*samavāya*), the establishment of inherence is not possible through the aforementioned inference; for it is more parsimonious to assume the status of a relation for the already established infinite individual essences (*svarūpa*) rather than for an infinite number of additional inherences.

Because of the propriety of [establishing] a relation, he himself states another means of proof (*pramāṇa*) even in that [opponent's] view for the sake of establishing inherence (*samavāya*), saying: "In this case... [and] "that which is inherent. The meaning is: "an effect that has its existence in something by way of inherence. [Rāmarudrī: In the absence of inherence, such a definition of an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) would be untenable.
The meaning of "that which is related" (*yatsambaddham*) is "the counter-correlate (*pratiyogī*) of a relation having [the substance] as its correlate (*anuyogika*).

Thus, since the relation enters [into the definition] precisely by virtue of being a relation, there is no failure of the definition of an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) even in the absence of inherence (*samavāya*); this is the intended sense. Regarding the phrase "proving what is already established" (*siddhasādhanam*), for whom [is it]?

Anticipating the objection that this would result in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), he says: "inseparable" (*ayuta*). Those two among which one subsists dependent upon the other are "inseparably established" (*ayutasiddha*). The purpose of the term "distinct entity" (*arthāntara*) is to establish a meaning not intended by [the opponent] himself. In that case as well—
Because the expectation "of what? arises, he says: "to inherence. "On account of parsimony" means:

on account of the cooperation of the knowledge of parsimony. Even from the inferential consideration (*parāmarśa*) that "it possesses the nature of being an effect, which is pervaded by being produced by an agent," there is parsimony in the unity of the agent (*kṛti*).

Just as there is an inference that "the earth, sprouts, and so forth are produced by a single creator" based on the cognition of parsimony (*lāghava*), so too— given that parsimony consists in the unity of the relation— it follows from the *parāmarśa* (inferential consideration) that "the cognition qualified by qualities, actions, and so forth possesses the property of being a qualified cognition, which is pervaded by having as its object the relation between the qualifier and the qualified," [arising] from the cognition of parsimony regarding the unity of the relation.

The collective meaning is that inference is that which has as its object a single relation between the qualifier and the qualified. If inherence were one, the Master [Udayana] would have raised the objection that air possesses color; however, that objection does not apply even to air, for it is only those who are deluded who perceive it so.

Since the cognition of possessing color [is not established] from this, he explains it as being for the purpose of establishing the validity of the cognition of possessing color—namely, "possessing color. He states the reason for that: "touch," etc. Regarding "the existence of the relation":
this refers to the existence of the relation between that [color] and its counter-correlate, by means of that very relation. (Rāmarudrī)
The sense is that [absence] pervades the locus of its own possessor (*tadvattva*) and does not exist where its counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) exists.
"Thus say the Navyas" means that, according to their view, there is no objection even if inherence (*samavāya*) were the relation for color (*rūpa*),
because they do not admit the inherence of color in air (*vāyu*).

If it were argued that even for non-existence (*abhāva*), a distinct relation (*saṃbandhāntara*) would have to be established as its qualification (*vaiśiṣṭya*), then— given that the term "distinct relation" in the root text refers to something other than conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and inherence (*samavāya*)— this would merely result in the acceptance of what is already desired, namely, that [the relation] is simply the essential nature (*svarūpa*) itself.

Because its relation [to the locus] is admitted, he therefore completes the remainder with the words "atirikta" (distinct/separate). It is accepted; the meaning is that it is acknowledged. Now, even when one absence of a jar has perished, the cognition of the existence of the absence of a jar in a place devoid of jars remains possible by taking another absence of a jar into account.
Anticipating this objection, he says: "delimited by potness" (*ghaṭatvāvacchinna*). Regarding the phrase "because of being of one kind":
the meaning is "because of being one. Regarding the phrase "of the cognition of the absence of a pot that is arising":
it refers to the erroneous [cognition] that occurs even on a ground possessing a pot during a state in which there is no knowledge of the presence of a pot.

Since the cognition "possessing the absence of a jar" certainly arises, that undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) is not possible; therefore, he establishes its status as valid knowledge by stating "pramātva" (validity). Anticipating the objection that this same reductio ad absurdum applies equally even to the view of those who maintain the oneness of inherence (samavāya), [the author] says:

He introduces the passage beginning with "mamatva" (the sense of "mine") with the word "nanu" (but surely). Regarding the second position, that of the impermanence of the specific qualification (*vaiśiṣṭya*): the meaning is that if one does not accept *vaiśiṣṭya*, one cannot accept a distinct relation between the absence and its locus.

He states the objection to the view that the essential nature (*svarūpa*) itself constitutes the relation: "If that were the case," etc. Regarding the phrase "that which belongs to the time of that [absence] on that particular ground," it is impossible for it to mean "belonging to the time when the absence of the jar exists on the ground," because [the relation would then apply] even during a state when the jar is present.

Since it is difficult to state a reason why [the absence] would not be present on the ground, he states the meaning of "belonging to that particular time" as "possessing the absence of the jar. In the phrase "belonging to the time of cognition," the word "cognition" refers to a cognition intended as valid knowledge (*pramā*); therefore, even during a state when the jar is present...

It should be noted that since the cognition of the absence of a jar as being of the nature of an error is possible, the aforementioned defect does not persist by taking that [cognition] into account. Now, one might raise the objection: "In this way, would it not contradict the established doctrine that the very nature (*svarūpa*) of the locus and the absentee constitutes their relation? To this [objection]:
He refutes [this objection] with the words "And thus" (*tathāca*). Regarding the phrase "a specific nature" (*svarūpaviśeṣa*):

the point is that since the intention of the statement "the relation is a specific nature" (*svarūpasaṃbandha*) is precisely that the relation is a specific nature, there is no contradiction with our own established doctrine (*siddhānta*). Regarding the phrase "The moderns, however" (*navyās tu*): [An objection is raised: But [in the case of] the ground...

Since the cognition "as in the absence of a jar" is accounted for by the relation of essential identity (*svarūpa-sambandha*) alone, there is no evidence for *vaiśiṣṭya* being a distinct category of reality; therefore, he says: "by the relation of essential identity.
The locus of the absence is the respective ground and so forth; the difference resides in that [locus] as an undivided whole.
[The definition is: the absence delimited by being the qualificandum of a valid cognition whose mode is "being different from that. Now, an objection:

if the aforementioned absence—which resides solely in each respective locus—is something distinct from that locus, then there would be the undesirable consequence of having to admit an infinite number of absences corresponding to each individual instance of a locus;
therefore, it is more appropriate to regard that absence as being of the very nature of the locus itself. Thus, by taking that [absence], [the definition does not fail].

Lest there be the consequence of an absence of a deciding factor (*vinigamanāviraha*), he says: "only that much" (*tāvanmātra*). In reality, however, there can be no absence of a deciding factor regarding the substrata along with the difference from the partless whole (*akhaṇḍa*), because, due to the multiplicity of the substrata, parsimony (*lāghava*) favors only a single difference.

Because of the appropriateness of its being a relation, he raises the objection of a lack of decisive evidence (*vinigamanāviraha*) by taking into account the cognition and so forth that have that [difference] as their object— beginning with the words "tāvanmātra" and so on. By this, it is shown that out of fear of infinite regress (*anavasthā*), one must accept that the difference residing in a locus is itself the nature of the locus, and not [any other].

The objection— that this would lead to the undesirable consequence of the dissolution of mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) itself, as in the case of the venerable teacher— is refuted. For if a specific cognition having substance, quality, and so forth as its object were related to the absence of substanceness (*dravyatvābhāva*),
then just as in the case of a quality, there would follow the cognition of the absence of substanceness even in a substance, since the cognition is of the nature of that relation.
Since [existence] is also present as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) in a substance (*dravya*), the word "only" (*mātra*) is used [to exclude it]. By the word "etc.

(*ādi*), desire (*icchā*) and so forth are included. And this is logical; for, in the view of the moderns who maintain that inherence (*samavāya*) is manifold, it is more parsimonious than postulating an infinite number of distinct and additional instances of inherence.

It should be understood that, since it is appropriate for only those things whose own natures are already established to function as relations, it follows that in his view an additional *samavāya* (inherence) is unestablished. Furthermore, by the phrase "here they say," a lack of satisfaction is indicated; the reason for this is that [the opponent's position fails] because of the various individual instances of cognition (*jñānavyakti*) directed toward that locus.

Considering the postulation of a relation, it is simpler (lāghava) to assume that a single instance of that cognition possesses such a nature; thus, there is no lack of a decisive criterion (vinigamanāviraha). For if only any one particular instance of cognition were so constituted, then in the absence of that specific cognitive instance, [the universal would not be perceived].

It should be understood that, due to the absence of a relation, there would be the consequence that no cognition qualified by an absence could arise; furthermore, if an eternal instance of knowledge were such [an entity], then because it has everything as its object, there would follow the undesirable consequence of a cognition of absence even where the counter-positive is present. || 11 ||
"It is simply the number six. Although, just as the difference between both a jar and a cloth [is not distinct from] each of the jar and the cloth individually, so it is here.
(Rāmarudrī)
If the absence of the difference delimited by "sixness" were [simply] non-existence, then since that [absence] exists in each individual substance (*dravya*) and so forth,

it would follow that those [substances] too would be non-existent. Nevertheless, even though the absence delimited by "sixness" exists in substances and so forth by way of the relation of pervasion (*paryāpti*), [this does not entail their non-existence] because of the "sixness" consisting of a collective increase (*apekṣābuddhi*).

It should be understood that because [the universal] acts as a delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) by way of being an object (*viṣayatā*), there is no unwanted consequence regarding positive entities (*bhāva*). Now, an objection:

there is a rule that properties (*dharma*) residing in multiple substrates (*vyāsajyavṛtti*) can only function as qualifiers (*prakāra*) through the relation of pervasion (*paryāpti*). Otherwise, since duality (*dvitva*) exists in each individual member by way of inherence (*samavāya*), a single person—[would also perceive it].
It cannot be argued that because the cognition "two" arises in dependence [on two things], and because even in the absence of the cognition "two," the cognition "one possesses duality" is accepted,
it is necessary for properties that exist distributively (vyāsajyavṛti) to function as qualifiers (prakāra) by way of inherence (samavāya). For in the cognition "possessing duality,"...

Since the meaning of the suffix *matup* (possessive) is itself the qualifier (*prakāra*), and since in the cognition "different from six" (*ṣaḍbhyo bhinnaḥ*) one experiences that the number six is the qualifier precisely through the relation of pervasion (*paryāpti*), the difference qualified by the number six is entirely without basis in valid cognition (*niṣprāmāṇika*). With this intention, he says: "In reality... (*vastutaḥ*).
"Thus it should be understood"—this means that its nature as an absence (*abhāvatva*) should be understood.

Although there is no fault whatsoever in the sixfold division of categories such as substance (*dravya*) being absences, nevertheless, due to the principle of parsimony (*lāghava*), and because the cognition of "absence-ness" occurs even when the six categories beginning with substance are unknown; [it is established that absence is a distinct category].
It should be understood that this has been set aside. He presents the view of those who maintain that "being an absence" (abhāvatva) is an indivisible (akhaṇḍa) upādhi, stating:
"In this regard, some say... [and] "of that which contains being an absence.
This refers to the case where mutual non-existence (anyonyābhāva) is defined merely as having a counter-correlativity (pratiyogitā) delimited by the relation of identity (tādātmya).

The point is that the inclusion of "non-existence" (abhāvatva) is necessary in order to avoid over-extension (ativyāpti) to such cases as "the difference from that which lacks pot-ness" (ghaṭatvābhāvavadbheda) with respect to pot-ness (ghaṭatva) and so forth.
[Regarding the phrase] "the occurrence of mutual dependence" (anyonyāśrayāpatti):...

The point is that the cognition of "being an absence" (abhāvatva) requires the cognition of "mutual absence-ness" (anyonyābhāvatva), and the cognition of "mutual absence-ness" requires the cognition of "being an absence. [Regarding the phrase] "the delimiting factor of the object of reference" (uddeśyatāvacchedaka) and so forth: [this applies] to the verbal cognition whose relation is identity (abheda).

The point is that, just as the identity between the delimitors of the subject (uddeśyatāvacchedaka) and the predicate (vidheyatāvacchedaka) [prevents verbal cognition], so too in a verbal cognition where the relation is difference (bhedasaṃsargaka), the identity between the subject-delimiter and the predicate is also a cause of the lack of expectancy (nirākāṅkṣatā).

Intending to show that the status of "non-existence-ness" (*abhāvatva*) as an indivisible limiting adjunct (*akhaṇḍopādhi*) cannot withstand scrutiny due to the absence of any means of proof (*pramāṇa*) for it, he says: "or else, it is a specific kind of relatum-ness (*anuyogitāviśeṣaḥ*). The word "specific" (*viśeṣa*) is used to exclude the relatum-ness of non-relational absences (*saṃsargābhāva*). [The reason for this is] the absence of proof (*pramāṇābhāva*).

Thus [it is said]. Now, one might object: "In the case of the absence of a jar and so forth, the very uniform cognition that 'this is an absence' will serve as the proof for its existence. Anticipating this doubt, he explains the uniform cognition by another means, beginning with "But rather... (kiṃtu).

[Objection: But in this way, since non-existence (abhāvatva) contains within it mutual non-existence (anyonyābhāva), the previously mentioned fallacy of circular reasoning (anyonyāśraya) would result;
therefore, he says: "due to inherence" (samavāya). The phrase "of the nature of non-existence with respect to existence" (satābhāvarūpa) has "non-existence-ness" (abhāvatvam) as its ellipsis.
[Objection: Even so, at a time when existence is not present, [the cognition] "this is a jar..."
Since the cognition of "it does not exist" and so forth would otherwise be untenable, he says: "And that... [tacceti]. Now, one might ask:
since there is parsimony (lāghava) in accepting that the specific property of being the counter-correlate (anuyogitā-viśeṣa) is itself non-existence (abhāvatva), why is that very thing not accepted?
To this he says: "And thus... [evañceti]. This means that there is a commonality (anugatatva) regarding the aspect of non-existence.

The meaning is that it consists in having a single property as its qualifier (*ekadharmaprakārakatva*). Thus, the point is that if non-existence (*abhāvatva*) were of the nature of a relatum (*anuyogitā*), then because that [relatum] would differ in each case—such as the absence of a jar—the cognition of non-existence would not possess a commonality (*anugatatva*).
Now, one might object that since it is impossible for a non-existent entity other than a universal (*jāti*) to appear by its own nature (*svarūpataḥ*), [how can this be so]?

One must admit that its being a qualifier (prakāratā) can only be stated by way of its very nature as an absence; and since that [absence] is of the nature of the absence of existence, that too must further be accepted as a qualifier by way of its being the absence of the absence of existence.
Thus, there arises the doubt that in the cognition of an absence, there would be an infinite regress of objective relations (viṣayatā).

He refutes this with the words "na ca" (nor). It should be understood that because the single absence of existence (*sattābhāva*) functions as a qualifier (*prakāra*) in various instances, it is not an infinite regress of objects (*viṣayānavasthā*) that is being stated, but rather an infinite regress of the object itself (*viṣayatānavasthā*). Now, even if one accepts that the absence of existence is a qualifier by its own nature (*svarūpataḥ*),...
At a time when existence (*sattā*) is not present, the cognition that "the jar does not exist" and so forth would be entirely untenable;

for since the knowledge of the counter-positive (*pratiyogijñāna*) is a cause for the knowledge of absence (*abhāva*), it is impossible for the absence of existence to appear without the knowledge of existence. Therefore, he says: "For this very reason," and "only in perception."

It is stated that [this is] perception because, in the case of verbal cognition whose object is a non-existence (*abhāva*), there is no requirement for the knowledge of the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*). As for "this": the object of perception is "this"; however, its being darkness is not of the nature of the absence of light, but rather simply the specific individuality (*tadvyaktitva*) residing in the absence of light.

For you, there is no impossibility of such a cognition without the knowledge of the qualifier (tejas). Now, [the opponent objects]: "If it is accepted that an absence which is existent but not previously present can function as a qualifier, then there would be a deviation (vyabhicāra) regarding the causal relation where the knowledge of the qualifier is the cause for a qualified cognition (viśiṣṭabuddhi) as delimited by the nature of being a qualified cognition. [Rāmarudrī]
Anticipating this objection, he says: "by means of the distinction of the qualifier. The underlying idea is as follows:

for the nature of a qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭabuddhitva*) is indeed distinct from the nature of a cognition possessing a mode (*saprakārakabuddhitva*), and the status of being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatva*) is also distinct from the status of being a mode (*prakāratva*). Thus, when the aforementioned causal relationship exists, [it follows] from the cognition of a jar...
Since the cognition of a cloth is also sometimes the qualifier for a jar,

one must therefore accept a specific causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) such that the cognition of a jar is the cause of the cognition qualified by a jar, and the cognition of a cloth is the cause of the cognition qualified by a cloth.

Regarding the word "therein" (*tatra*): it means in the cognition qualified by the property of being an absence (*abhāvatva*). Regarding the phrase "as its cause" (*taddhetutve*): it means because the cognition of the property of being an absence is not accepted as a cause [of that cognition].
Now, one might object: "What is the reason for not postulating the cognition of the qualifier as a cause in every case of a qualified cognition?
To this, he says: "the result," etc. Without the cognition of the qualifier...

The result is the non-arising of a qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭabuddhi*). This means that the postulation of the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) is based on following that [result]. Since a qualified cognition of a jar or the like does not arise without the cognition of the jar itself, the causal relation is postulated in that case.

The meaning is that it is not postulated here because of the arising of a cognition qualified by the absence of non-presence (*anupasthita-abhāvatva*). Regarding the phrase "at the end of a *dvandva*": now, the analysis (*vigraha*) here as "conjunction (*saṃsarga*) and mutual [relation] (*anyonya*), and those two are both conjunction and mutual [relation], and those two are both absences (*abhāva*)" is not possible.

Since it is not accepted that conjunction (*saṃsarga*) is a type of non-existence (*abhāva*), the term "conjunction" here does not refer to a relation other than identity (*tādātmya*), and the term "mutuality" (*anyonya*) refers to the relation of identity; thus,
by the etymological derivation "non-existences [defined] by means of conjunction and mutuality," the term "mutuality" indeed refers to the relation of identity.

And thus, it should not be argued that there is no such fault because, by the etymological derivation "absence [consisting of] relation and mutual [non-existence]," one obtains both the absence whose counter-positiveness is delimited by a relation other than identity and the absence whose counter-positiveness is delimited by identity itself—
since the third case-ending (tṛtīyā) signifies "having a counter-positiveness delimited by [the preceding term]. Even so, [the fault remains].

If it is argued that there would be the undesirable consequence of failing to include destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) and prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) under the view that their counter-positiveness (*pratiyogitva*) is not delimited by a relation, we say no; for the word "relation" (*saṃsarga*) refers to a relation in the sense of a counter-positiveness not delimited by identity (*tādātmya*), while the word "mutuality" (*anyonya*)— [...is used in the sense of a relation delimited by identity.]

There is no inconsistency, because by the etymological analysis "the two absences [are those] whose counterpositiveness is delimited by identity," one obtains the meaning "the two absences that have as their qualifiers those two aforementioned counterpositives. This is because the genitive case here signifies the very relation of being a qualifier (*nirūpakatva*). Alternatively, the word *saṃsarga* (relation) may be understood as referring to the word *saṃsarga* preceded by [the word *tādātmya*].

The term *anyonya-pada* (the word "mutual") refers to that which precedes the word "negation" (*abhāva*), and the term *abhāva-pada* (the word "negation") refers to that which is denoted by the word "negation.

Thus, through the etymological analysis (*vyutpatti*) that they are both "mutuality" and "negations," the resulting meaning obtained is: "those two which are denoted by the compound term 'negation of mutual relation' (*saṃsargānyonya-padapūrvakābhāva-pada-vācya*)."

By this, the objection that—since the definition of the two types of absence is already obtained from the aforementioned statement itself—the subsequent presentation of the definitions of the two absences is irrelevant due to a lack of expectancy—is also refuted. The same applies to what follows. Furthermore, in the definition of mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*), the term "absence" (*abhāva*) is used precisely to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to positive entities (*bhāva*). [The phrase] "by way of identity" (*tādātmyatvena*)...

Identity (*tādātmyatva*) is the unique property residing in that [identity]. He states the result of intending [the definition] as being delimited by identity (*tādātmyāvacchinnatva*) through the word "by that" (*tena*). Regarding the phrase "the absolute absence of the conjunct" (*saṃyogyatyantābhāva*): since the identity with the conjunct (*saṃyogi-tādātmya*) has the nature of conjunction (*saṃyoga*), [the absence of the conjunct is the absence of that identity].
In the case of absolute absence whose counter-correlativity is delimited by the relation of conjunction (*saṃyoga*),
there is over-extension (*ativyāpti*) according to the literal reading; however,

[the definition now applies] to that delimitation-in-the-mode-of-relation (*saṃsargavidhayāvacchedakatā*) residing in identity (*tādātmya*), which is delimited by the state of being identical (*tādātmyatva*).

The point is that, by obtaining the state of having a counter-correlativity determined by that [property], the delimitation of the counter-correlativity residing in conjunction within absolute absence is delimited solely by the nature of conjunction (*saṃyogatva*); therefore, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*). Although...

Since the identity of the conjoined (*saṃyogitādātmya*) consists in the nature of conjunction, its being an identity would itself be nothing other than conjunction; thus, the exclusion of over-extension (*ativyāpti`) remains difficult to achieve. Nevertheless, the "identity-ness" (*tādātmyatva*) that delimits relation-ness (*saṃsargatāvacchedaka*) is not of the form of conjunction-ness (*saṃyogatva*) and so forth, but rather simply the state of being a unique property residing in the conjoined entities and so on.

Therefore, since in the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) of absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*), conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) precisely by way of its nature as conjunction, and not by way of being an uncommon property (*asādhāraṇadharma*), there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in that case;
for it is only the relation that delimits the counter-correlativity of difference (*bhedapratiyogitāvacchedakasambandha*) which constitutes an uncommon property.

The sense is that [the distinction between] absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) and mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) would be impossible otherwise, because [non-existence] is admitted to be a positive entity (*bhāva*). "Its establishment" means the inference of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*).
And the method of that inference is as follows: "This jar is produced by causes that do not exist at the moment of its own production."

The meaning is that the prior non-existence (prāgabhāva) is established through the force of inference in the form "because it has not arisen in the second moment of its own production," since this sublates other [theories]; for that [prior non-existence] is destroyed by the causal complex (sāmagrī) and therefore does not subsist at the moment of the production of its counter-positive (pratiyogin).

He sets forth the opinion of the authors of the *Dīdhiti* with the words "some" (*kecit*). The phrase "of people" (*lokānām*) means "of those common to both the learned (*paṇḍita*) and the ignorant (*pāmara*).
[ie3]
The point is that if prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) were perceptible, it would follow that even common people (*pāmara*) would perceive it.
Nor can it be argued that the very cognition "the jar will come into existence" is the proof for prior non-existence.
It should not be argued that "future-ness" consists simply in being the counter-positive of the prior absence (*prāgabhāva*) of the present;

for we accept that "future-ness" consists rather in having an origination at a time that is the locus of the destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) of the present time. And origination is the relation with the first moment. Furthermore, the "first-ness" of a moment is—

The intended meaning is: "the state of not being the locus of the destruction of the moment that is the locus of that [prior absence]. Regarding the phrase "of that which is established as a generator": one should not raise the objection, "Why should the absence of substance be postulated as a cause for a produced substance by one who maintains that prior absence (*prāgabhāva*) is the cause? For where...

Immediately after the destruction of this jar, another jar is produced from the two potsherds that constitute its cause; for otherwise, it would be impossible to prevent the production of yet another jar at the second moment following the production of the previous jar.
This is because the pot-sherd conjunctions and other factors that serve as the causes for the production of that specific pot are present at that time.

Nor should it be argued that such a consequence does not arise because the specific conjunction of the two shards that initiates the second pot is absent then; for what is being proposed here is not the production of a second pot-individual.
It cannot be said that its occurrence is avoided because of the absence of a specific instance of the conjunction with that potsherd;

nor can it be said that the occurrence of the previous pot-instance is not entailed because of the absence of its prior non-existence; rather, what is entailed is simply the occurrence of that which is delimited by the universal "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*).

The objection is that [the production of the pot] would follow because all its causes, such as the prior non-existence (prāgabhāva) of the pot, are present. As for the point that where the production of a broken pot is to occur,
even at a time when a large pot exists, the production of that broken pot would result from the force of its prior non-existence and so forth— [this is raised] to prevent such an occurrence.

The claim that the absence of a substance must necessarily be a cause is baseless; for it should be understood that such an implication cannot arise, since the destruction of a large jar is the cause of a broken jar.
[This refers to] "of such an absence of a substance."
The meaning is: "of the absence of substance whose counterpositiveness is delimited by inherence.

Regarding the phrase "of such absences of destruction": the meaning is "of those absences of destruction that arise at the time of the production of a produced substance. And here... [end of fragment]

By means of the plural number, with respect to the absence of a substance, the absence of such a destruction is more complex; therefore, there is no lack of a deciding factor (*vinigamanāviraha*) by taking causality in that form. Rather, it is with respect to each particular substance that the individual instances of destruction produced at the time of its production [are the causes].
Therefore, it is indicated that the causality of non-existence must be stated precisely as its specific individuality (*tattadvyaktitvena*);

thus, because there would otherwise be an infinite number of cause-and-effect relations, there is no lack of a determining principle (*vinigamanāviraha*). Nor should it be argued that, in that case, the causality of destructions (*dhvaṃsa*) and absences (*abhāva*) is itself without justification.

In the view of those who do not accept absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) as residing in the locus of prior non-existence of destruction (*dhvaṃsa-prāgabhāva*), one must, out of necessity, abandon the non-existence of substances and accept that the non-existences consisting of destruction (*dhvaṃsābhāva*) possess causality; for otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that produced substances could never arise. And thus, of that which has arisen...
To prevent re-emergence, if prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) is not accepted, the proponents of novelty must postulate the causality of the non-existence of substances (*dravyābhāva*),

while the ancient proponents of destruction-non-existence (*dhvaṃsābhāva*) must likewise postulate it for their respective non-existences; however, the proponent of prior non-existence, disregarding all that, postulates prior non-existence alone as the cause.
That is the intention of that book. In reality, however, since the absence of substance (dravyābhāva) established by inherence—
which is admitted by both disputants— is to be accepted as a cause by virtue of being a cause for that which is delimited by the nature of a produced substance (janyadravyatvāvacchinna),
the word ending in the genitive case [in the term "abhāvāt"] here also [refers to that].
Furthermore, the meaning obtained is that there is an absence of a substance established through positive concomitance (*anvaya*). Thus,

even if the proponent of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) does not admit that the substance acts as an inhibitor, it is more appropriate to state that the cause is simply the absence of the substance— since that is what is established by observation— and not something unestablished.

The phrase "of prior non-existence" (prāgabhāvasya) refers to the meaning of the preceding text. And thus, at the time of the production of a jar from the conjunction of two potsherds, the production of the jar must be admitted even in the case of the potsherd-fragments (kāpālikā) and so forth; otherwise, [the jar] would not exist by way of inherence (samavāya) in the potsherd-fragment.

Because it would entail the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of the perception of the absence of a jar [even when it exists], one must state that the cause is precisely the absence of a substance that does not initiate that particular substance. And thus, we consider it correct that the suspicion regarding the attribution of causality to the absences of various specific destructions (dhvaṃsa) is indeed well-founded, due to the lack of a decisive criterion (vinigamanāviraha). Thus...

Even though there exist such objections as follows: if the absence of destruction at the time of the production of a substance were the cause for the production of another substance, then after the destruction of a particular jar, no other jar could be produced from its constituent potsherds, because the required cause— the absence of such a destruction— would be lacking.
Setting aside those [arguments] because they are obvious, he states another refutation, beginning with "prāgabhāva" (prior non-existence).
Here, the phrase "they say" implies that it refers to the followers of the ancients. "Tatsaṃyogānām" means "of the conjunctions of the threads. Then, "even so" refers to the prior non-existence.

The meaning is: "even if [the non-existence] were the cause. Regarding the phrase "the consequence of [the production of] origination": the remainder of the sense is that since you do not accept the causality of those specific instances of conjunction, the prior non-existence (prāgabhāva) would still exist at that time. [This applies to] those specific instances of conjunction.

The sense is that if [the prior non-existence] is accepted as being the cause, the postulation of a prior non-existence (prāgabhāva) is redundant. "In those which are not its own substrata" means in those which are not the substrata of a cloth made of a thousand threads.
"Even in another thread" [is the meaning].
